message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is an overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24) and related statutes: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• Landlord must return the deposit within 30 days after the tenant vacates, unless the landlord provides a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs you pay yourself. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition and keep all structural elements, plumbing, heating, and electrical systems in good working order.
• Landlord must repair any major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems promptly in writing; keep copies of all communications. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Tenant has the right to use the premises without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (see next). | | **Notice of Entry** | • Landlord must give at least 24‑hour written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | • If the landlord enters without notice, you may withhold rent or sue for damages. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlord may increase rent only at the end of a lease term, and the increase must be in writing. | • A landlord cannot raise rent mid‑lease without a valid reason (e.g., a new lease). | | **Lease Termination** | • Landlord must provide a written notice of termination at least 30 days before the end of the lease term. | • If the landlord fails to give notice, the lease may be extended automatically. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | • Tenants can file complaints with the Texas Commission on Human Rights if discrimination occurs. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect within a reasonable time after notice, the tenant may repair it themselves and deduct the cost from rent (subject to certain limits). | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the proper eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment), file a lawsuit, obtain a judgment, and then obtain a writ of possession. | • Tenants can contest eviction in court; they may also negotiate a settlement. | | **Right to Retain Rent** | • If the landlord fails to provide essential services (heat, hot water, etc.) for a period of 7 days, the tenant may withhold rent until the issue is resolved. | • Document the lack of service and communicate with the landlord. | | **Right to Repair** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect within a reasonable time after notice, the tenant may repair it themselves and deduct the cost from rent (subject to certain limits). | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required by law, a written lease clarifies the terms and protects both parties. | • Tenants should always sign a written lease and keep a copy. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, any written notices, emails, text messages, and photos of any damage or maintenance issues. 2. **Serve Notices Properly** – If you need to give notice to your landlord (e.g., to terminate the lease or to request repairs), do so in writing and keep a copy. 3. **Know the Time Frames** – Texas law specifies how long a landlord has to respond to repair requests and how much notice is required for entry or termination. 4. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you believe your landlord is violating your rights, consult a local attorney or a tenant advocacy organization. The Texas Attorney General’s Office and local legal aid societies can provide guidance. ### Resources - **Texas Property Code, Chapter 24** – The statutory framework for residential leases. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – Handles discrimination complaints. - **Texas Attorney General’s Office** – Provides consumer protection resources. - **Local Legal Aid** – Many counties offer free or low‑cost legal assistance to tenants. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal questions, consult a licensed attorney in Texas.
